#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The path module has a few different functions: Clean, Split, Join, Ext, Dir, Base, IsAbs. These functions do not take into account the OS-specific path separator, meaning that they won't behave as intended on Windows.

For example, Dir is supposed to return all but the last element of the path. For the path ``C:\some\dir\somewhere``, it is supposed to return ``C:\some\dir\``, however, it returns ``.``.

Instead of these functions, the ones in filepath should be used instead.

issue_context.title: path functions not working as intended on Windows
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The ``path`` module has a few different functions: Clean, Split, Join, Ext, Dir, Base, IsAbs. These functions do not take into account the OS-specific path separator, meaning that they won't behave as intended on Windows. The ``path`` should not be used for file paths.

For example, Dir is supposed to return all but the last element of the path. For the path ``C:\some\dir\somewhere``, it is supposed to return ``C:\some\dir\``, however, it returns ``.``.


### What did you expect to happen?

Instead of these functions, the ones in ``filepath`` should be used instead.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Example:

```
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"path"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Comparing path.Operation\t to\t filepath.Operation on Windows.\n")

	// Clean should remove duplicate slashes and evaluate the ..
	folder := `C:\\some\dir\\\\somewhere\\..\`
	fmt.Printf("Clean: %s \t\t %s\n", path.Clean(folder), filepath.Clean(folder))

	// Split should give us the base folder and the file.
	file := `C:\\some\dir\\somewhere.txt`
	dir1, f1 := path.Split(file)
	dir2, f2 := filepath.Split(file)
	fmt.Printf("Split: %s, %s \t\t %s, %s\n", dir1, f1, dir2, f2)

	// Join should use the oS-specific path separator.
	fmt.Printf("Join: %s \t\t %s\n", path.Join(file, "foo"), filepath.Join(file, "foo"))

	// Ext should give us the file extension.
	fmt.Printf("Ext: %s \t\t %s\n", path.Ext(file), filepath.Ext(file))

	// Base should return the last element of the path.
	fmt.Printf("Base: %s \t\t %s\n", path.Base(file), filepath.Base(file))

	// Dir should return all but the last element of the path.
	fmt.Printf("Dir: %s \t\t %s\n", path.Dir(file), filepath.Dir(file))

	// IsAbs should return True in this case, as it is an absolute path.
	fmt.Printf("IsAbs: %t \t\t %t\n", path.IsAbs(file), filepath.IsAbs(file))
}
```

```
PS C:\> go version
go version go1.18.2 windows/amd64

PS C:\> go run .\pather_windows.go
Comparing path.Operation         to      filepath.Operation on Windows.

Clean: C:\\some\dir\\\\somewhere\\..\            C:\some\dir
Split: , C:\\some\dir\\somewhere.txt             C:\\some\dir\\, somewhere.txt
Join: C:\\some\dir\\somewhere.txt/foo            C:\some\dir\somewhere.txt\foo
Ext: .txt                .txt
Base: C:\\some\dir\\somewhere.txt                somewhere.txt
Dir: .           C:\\some\dir\
IsAbs: false             true
```

review_comments:
The blow is using `!strings.HasPrefix(*field, "/")`, and the comment change seems to be wrong.

We should remove the comments here and change the below if statement to use `filepath.IsAbs()` according to https://github.com/golang/go/issues/1483.

I disagree. The point in this comment is that for some reason ``/``-prefixed paths are not considered absolute paths in Windows golang, even though it is considered as an absolute path in other languages, and it is considered an absolute path (relative to the current drive letter) in Windows in general [1]. I have another PR open for something relate to absolute / relative paths. [2]

So, there are 2 outcomes of this function:

- the field starts with ``/``, and thus, an absolute path. In this case, it will prepend the drive letter to it.
- the field doesn't start with ``/``, in which case it is a noop.

If we'd use ``!filepath.IsAbs(*field)`` instead of ``!strings.HasPrefix(*field, "/"``, the 2 cases would instead do as follows:

- the field starts with ``/``, which technically is an absolute path, but ``filepath.IsAbs`` would return ``false``. This means that the function does nothing.
- the field doesn't start with ``/``, in which case ``filepath.IsAbs`` returns false, in which case it is a noop.

If we'd change ``strings.HasPrefix`` with ``filepath.IsAbs``, we'd have a regression.

[1] https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file#fully-qualified-vs-relative-paths
[2] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112566
i can confirm windows has the abs / driveletter problem in go's stdlib.
